propositions.text: Applicant seeks a stay of removal from Canada until judicial review is finally disposed of
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks an order staying her removal from Canada, currently scheduled for Friday, November 26, 2021, until her Application for Leave and for Judicial Review is finally disposed of.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks a stay of removal from Canada until judicial review is finally disposed of.

propositions.text: Underlying application relates to negative decision on Applicant's permanent residence request on humanitarian and compassionate grounds
propositions.quote: The underlying application is in relation to a negative decision on the Applicant’s request for permanent residence in Canada on humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds issued on January 6, 2021, by a Senior Immigration Officer.

propositions.text: Application for Leave and for Judicial Review filed February 8, 2021, perfected July 15, 2021
propositions.quote: The Application for Leave and for Judicial Review was filed on February 8, 2021, and was perfected for a leave determination by the Court on July 15, 2021.

propositions.text: Applicant received Direction to Report for removal on October 20, 2021; motion filed October 28, 2021
propositions.quote: The Applicant received a Direction to Report for removal on October 20, 2021, and this motion was filed on October 28, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: Court states underlying application is a negative H&C decision; judicial review filed and perfected; removal direction and motion dates given.

propositions.text: Applicant is 44-year-old Indian citizen, permanent resident since 2010 as spouse of skilled worker
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 44 year old citizen of India who entered Canada as a Permanent Resident in December 2010, as the spouse of a member of the skilled worker class.

propositions.text: Report under s 44 IRPA for serious criminality issued August 17, 2015; deportation order September 28, 2018; Applicant lost permanent resident status
propositions.quote: On August 17, 2015, a report was issued under s 44 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c 27 [IRPA] for serious criminality contrary to s 36(1)(a) of IRPA. As a result, a deportation order was issued on September 28, 2018, and the Applicant lost her permanent resident status.

propositions.text: H&C application submitted June 5, 2019
propositions.quote: The H&C application was submitted on June 5, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Applicant's background: Indian citizen, permanent resident since 2010, serious criminality report and deportation, H&C application date.

propositions.text: Serious criminality was manslaughter conviction with 10-year sentence on July 31, 2015
propositions.quote: The serious criminality cited in the s 44 Report was the Applicant’s conviction for manslaughter for which she received a sentence on July 31, 2015, of 10 years imprisonment with credit for several months of pre-trial custody.

paragraphs.summary: Court states serious criminality was manslaughter conviction with 10-year sentence.

propositions.text: Crime was appalling; victim was 3-year-old child with massive brain injury and multiple injuries
propositions.quote: It was an appalling crime. As set out in the Reasons for Sentence of the trial judge, in September 2011, the Applicant’s three year old child sustained a massive brain injury as a result of blunt force trauma to her skull.

propositions.text: Victim's body had dozens of internal and external injuries predating death; hospital condition was horrific
propositions.quote: In addition to the fatal injuries suffered, her body was riddled with dozens of internal and external injuries that included bruising, hemorrhaging and multiple skull fractures which predated the date of her death. The description of her condition upon arrival at the hospital is horrific.

paragraphs.summary: Court describes appalling crime: 3-year-old child victim with massive brain injury and multiple injuries.

propositions.text: Applicant charged with second-degree murder for repeated beatings; jury convicted manslaughter, implying killing was not intentional
propositions.quote: The Applicant was charged with second-degree murder on the basis of allegations that she had beat her daughter over many weeks or months culminating in the final fatal attack. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter, thus presumably accepting that the killing was not-intentional.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Applicant was charged with second-degree murder but jury convicted manslaughter, implying no intent.

propositions.text: Sentencing judge noted aggravating factors: victim vulnerability, repeated assaults, denial of responsibility, lack of remorse
propositions.quote: The sentencing judge noted that there were numerous aggravating factors to the crime including the vulnerability of the victim, the evidence of repeated assaults, the offender’s denial of responsibility and lack of empathy or remorse for the loss of her daughter.

propositions.text: No family spoke for the child; court did so; no mitigating factors
propositions.quote: No one from the immediate or extended family spoke for the child. It was left for the Court to do so. There were no mitigating factors.

propositions.text: Facts not necessary for motion but stated because Applicant may not have accepted responsibility and family claims she is blameless
propositions.quote: These facts are not necessary for the determination of this motion but I think it is necessary that they be stated because it is not at all clear that the Applicant has accepted responsibility for her crime and members of her family continue to claim she is blameless.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes aggravating factors, no mitigating factors, and doubts about Applicant's acceptance of responsibility.

propositions.text: Sentencing court noted conviction's immigration consequences and gave modest weight in sentencing
propositions.quote: The Sentencing Court noted that the conviction would result in significant immigration consequences for the Applicant and gave that factor some modest weight in determining sentence.

propositions.text: Applicant notes deportation should not be additional punishment
propositions.quote: The Applicant properly notes that deportation should not be considered an additional punishment for her crime.

propositions.text: Applicant benefitted somewhat from immigration consequences being considered in sentence length
propositions.quote: Nonetheless, she has benefitted to some extent from it being taken into account in the length of incarceration imposed.

paragraphs.summary: Court states sentencing court considered immigration consequences; Applicant argues deportation not punishment; Applicant benefitted from this consideration.

propositions.text: Applicant had two other children removed at birth; they and older child live with father and grandmother
propositions.quote: Pending trial, the Applicant had two other children with her husband, both of whom were removed from their care at birth by the Children’s Aid Society. They, and an older child born before the victim, live with their father and their grandmother.

propositions.text: Applicant released on parole to half-way house with strict conditions including no contact with minors unless supervised
propositions.quote: The Applicant has now been released on parole to live in a half-way house under strict conditions including that she has no contact with anyone under the age of 16 including her own children unless accompanied by a responsible adult approved in advance by her parole supervisor.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Applicant's other children removed; Applicant on parole with strict no-contact conditions with minors.

propositions.text: Applicant filed extensive updated submissions for H&C application between June 2019 and September 2020
propositions.quote: The Applicant filed extensive updated submissions in support of her H&C application between the initial filing on June 4, 2019, and September 25, 2020.

propositions.text: Applicant's April 5, 2019 affidavit diminishes responsibility despite jury verdict and trial judge findings
propositions.quote: I note that in the Applicant’s affidavit sworn on April 5, 2019, in support of her H&C application, she continues to diminish her responsibility for the crime notwithstanding the jury verdict and the trial judge’s factual findings about the abuse inflicted on the child.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Applicant filed updated submissions and affidavit diminishing responsibility despite verdict and findings.

propositions.text: Submissions included letters of support and rehabilitation reports
propositions.quote: In addition to written representations, the submissions included letters of support from family, friends and caseworkers and reports of rehabilitation programs completed by the Applicant while incarcerated.

propositions.text: Grounds included establishment and family ties, best interests of surviving children, hardship in India
propositions.quote: The grounds relied upon in support of the application included her degree of establishment and family ties in Canada, the best interests of her surviving children and hardship to be expected from conditions in India.

propositions.text: Applicant says she is Brahmin but would not be accepted in husband's family due to strict cultural norms
propositions.quote: While the Applicant is, as she noted in her affidavit, a Brahmin and therefore a member of the highest caste in Hindu society, she says she would not be accepted in her husband’s family because of the strict cultural norms in their community.

paragraphs.summary: Court states submissions included support letters, rehabilitation reports, and grounds including family ties and hardship; Applicant alleges caste rejection.

propositions.text: Senior Immigration Officer reviewed background, offence nature, and Applicant's materials
propositions.quote: The Senior Immigration Officer who considered the application reviewed the background, nature of the offence and the materials submitted on behalf of the Applicant.

propositions.text: Officer addressed each ground raised by Applicant
propositions.quote: The Officer addressed each of the grounds raised by the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker reviewed background, offence, and addressed each ground raised by Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer erred by applying incorrect test on circumstances, establishment, best interests, and hardship
propositions.quote: On this motion, the Applicant argues that the Officer made several errors notably in application of an incorrect test in assessing the Applicant’s circumstances and degree of establishment, in considering the best interests of the surviving children and the evidence of hardship the Applicant claims she would face in India.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer erred by applying incorrect test on circumstances, establishment, best interests, and hardship.

propositions.text: Issues: anonymization order and interlocutory injunction test
propositions.quote: The issues to be addressed on this motion are as follows: A. Whether the Court should make an Anonymization Order? B. Whether the Applicant has satisfied the test for an interlocutory injunction?

paragraphs.summary: Court states issues: anonymization order and interlocutory injunction test.

propositions.text: Applicant requests anonymization order for herself, husband, and children in public documents
propositions.quote: By notice filed on October 28, 2021, the Applicant requested that the Court make an order that all documents that are prepared by the Court and which may be made available to the public be amended and redacted to the extent necessary to make the identity of the Applicant, her husband and their three children anonymous.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant requests anonymization order for herself, husband, and children in public documents.

propositions.text: Applicant submits media attention and publication of names may harm children's health and cause distress
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the criminal trial garnered substantial media attention. Publication of the names of her and her family members in relation to her Federal Court case may be harmful to her children’s mental, physical, and emotional health. Any ongoing publicity may cause additional distress to her children.

propositions.text: Trial judge imposed publication ban on names of surviving children
propositions.quote: The trial judge imposed a ban on publication of the names of any surviving children of the Applicant and her husband in relation to the case.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits media attention and publication may harm children; trial judge imposed publication ban on children's names.

propositions.text: Respondent notes strong presumption of open courts and high bar for anonymization or redaction orders
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that there is a strong presumption in favour of open courts and that there is a high bar against such a request for a discretionary court order, including redactions of identifying information, in order to maintain the open court principle: Sherman Estate v Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 at paras 2-3.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues strong open court presumption and high bar for anonymization or redaction orders.

propositions.text: Applicant's anonymization request is overly broad as crime facts are public
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the Applicant’s request is overly broad particularly in as much as the facts of the crime and the conviction are already known to the public.

propositions.text: If only Applicant concerned, request would be refused
propositions.quote: Were it to only concern the Applicant, I would have no hesitation in refusing the request.

propositions.text: Request also concerns children who suffered from publicity, so limited order appropriate
propositions.quote: However, it also concerns her children and I am satisfied from the evidence submitted that the oldest child in particular suffered from the publicity about her mother’s actions.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant's request overly broad but limited order appropriate due to children's suffering from publicity.

propositions.text: Court orders anonymization of Applicant's name by initials in style of cause; no order for redaction of family identities now
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that a more limited order would suffice and I will therefore order that the name of the Applicant in the style of cause on this motion and in any subsequent proceedings be anonymized by the substitution of initials for her full name. There will be on order for redaction of the identities of the Applicant and her family members but that question could be revisited should leave be granted and the matter proceed to judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Court orders anonymization of Applicant's name by initials; no redaction of family identities now but may revisit later.

propositions.text: Stay motion requires conjunctive tripartite test: serious issue, irreparable harm, balance of convenience
propositions.quote: To be successful on a stay motion, the Applicant must satisfy the conjunctive tripartite test, set out in Manitoba (Attorney General) v Metropolitan Stores Ltd.,[1987] 1 S.C.R. 110 and applied by the Federal Court of Appeal to stays of deportation in Toth v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1988), 86 N.R. 302 (F.C.A.) [Toth], namely that there is a serious issue to be tried, that the Applicant would suffer irreparable harm if a stay is not granted and that as between the parties, the balance of convenience lies in the Applicant’s favour.

propositions.text: Principles confirmed by Supreme Court in RJR MacDonald and R v Canadian Broadcasting Corp
propositions.quote: These principles were confirmed by the Supreme Court in RJR MacDonald Inc. v Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 SCR 311 and R v Canadian Broadcasting Corp, 2018 SCC 5, [2018] 1 SCR 196, at para 12.

paragraphs.summary: Court states stay motion requires tripartite test confirmed by Supreme Court.

propositions.text: The threshold for a serious issue to be tried is low; the case must not be frivolous or vexatious and only minimal inquiry is needed.
propositions.quote: The threshold for determining whether there is a serious issue to be tried is low. The Court must be satisfied that the case is neither frivolous nor vexatious. A prolonged inquiry into the merits is neither necessary nor desirable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the low threshold for a serious issue to be tried requires only minimal inquiry and the case must not be frivolous or vexatious.

propositions.text: The Officer erred by assessing circumstances only through hardship and wrongly applied exceptionality in the relief test.
propositions.quote: the Applicant argues that the Officer erred in assessing the Applicant’s circumstances exclusively through the lens of hardship and by importing exceptionality into the test for relief

propositions.text: The Officer erred by applying hardship as the test for best interests of surviving children, contrary to Supreme Court requirements.
propositions.quote: the Officer erred in applying hardship as the test in his assessment of the best interests of the surviving children. He was not, it is argued, “alert, alive and sensitive to their best interest” as required by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Kanthasamy

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Officer erred by focusing only on hardship and misapplying the test for children's best interests.

propositions.text: The H&C decision is reasonable; the Officer considered all factors and gave reasons for refusal on each.
propositions.quote: the Respondent contends that the H&C decision is reasonable as the Officer considered each of the factors raised by the Applicant and provided reasons in the decision for refusing the application on each factor

propositions.text: The Respondent addresses each of the Applicant’s arguments about the Officer’s alleged errors in turn.
propositions.quote: The Respondent addresses each of the Applicant’s arguments about the Officer’s alleged errors in turn

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Officer's decision was reasonable and addresses each applicant's alleged error.

propositions.text: The Officer’s reasons are thorough but the court will only do minimal inquiry to see if arguments are frivolous or vexatious.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the Officer’s reasons are thorough but it is not the Court’s role on a motion such as this to assess the merits of the arguments advanced by the Applicant beyond the minimal inquiry necessary to determine whether they are frivolous or vexatious

propositions.text: The Applicant’s arguments do constitute serious issues to be tried.
propositions.quote: I am unable to conclude that the arguments presented by the Applicant do not constitute serious issues to be tried

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer’s reasons thorough and that the applicant’s arguments raise serious issues to be tried.

propositions.text: Applicant submits she will face irreparable harm if removed before judicial review, citing Toth decision on family business harm.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the second branch of the test for a stay or injunction is whether she will face irreparable harm ... She points to the conclusion in Toth, above: … I am of the view that the applicant has met the irreparable harm test

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submits she will face irreparable harm if removed before judicial review, citing Toth decision.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Federal Court of Appeal decisions requiring clear evidence of real probability of irreparable harm, not mere likelihood.
propositions.quote: To establish irreparable harm, there must be evidence at a convincing level of particularity that demonstrates a real probability that unavoidable irreparable harm will result unless a stay is granted

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues irreparable harm requires clear evidence of real probability, not just reasonable likelihood.

propositions.text: Justice Norris described irreparable harm as real, definite, unavoidable harm, not hypothetical or speculative, requiring clear evidence.
propositions.quote: [22] Under the second part of the test for a stay, “the only issue to be decided is whether a refusal to grant relief could so adversely affect the applicants’ own interests that the harm could not be remedied if the eventual decision on the merits does not accord with the result of the interlocutory application” ... [24] To establish irreparable harm, the applicant must show that there is “real, definite, unavoidable harm – not hypothetical and speculative harm”

propositions.text: Irreparable harm concerns harm's nature, not magnitude, and must be shown with convincing particularity.
propositions.quote: This is what is meant by describing the harm that must be established as “irreparable”. It concerns the nature of the harm rather than its magnitude ... there must be evidence at a convincing level of particularity that demonstrates a real probability that unavoidable irreparable harm will result

paragraphs.summary: Justice Norris explained irreparable harm requires real, definite, unavoidable harm with clear evidence, focusing on harm's nature not magnitude.

propositions.text: Applicant submits she and children face irreparable harm from removal; family would not follow to India; children deprived of daily contact.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that she and her children will face irreparable harm from her removal. It appears now that the family would not follow her to India ... The children would be deprived of the daily contact they presently have with their mother

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submits removal would cause irreparable harm as family would not follow and children lose daily contact.

propositions.text: Applicant argues oldest child has disorders worsened by removal; she has mental disorders needing treatment unavailable in India; supported by psychologist reports.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues further that the oldest child suffers from disorders ... and her health would deteriorate if her mother were removed. The Applicant contends that she also suffers from mental disorders ... supported by psychologist reports and other evidence

propositions.text: Removal would separate applicant from family for extended time; she cannot return without pardon and approval; pardon unavailable for 10 years.
propositions.quote: Removal, the Applicant argues, would result in her being separated from her family for an extended period of time ... She will remain ineligible for a pardon for another 10 years

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues removal harms oldest child's health and her own mental health, causing extended family separation due to pardon ineligibility.

propositions.text: Removal would render judicial review proceedings illusory and reduce chances of success if readmitted later; harm from separation would have occurred.
propositions.quote: The Applicant contends that should she be removed, the proceedings before this Court ... will be rendered illusory ... the chances of success ... would be substantially reduced ... the harm resulting from her separation from the family would have already occurred

paragraphs.summary: The applicant contends removal would make judicial review illusory and reduce success chances, with harm from family separation.

propositions.text: Applicant could rely on extended family in India and maintain ties via technology; mootness does not establish irreparable harm warranting stay.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Applicant could rely on her extended family in India for support and maintain ties with her family through the use of modern technology. Any potential mootness ... does not, in itself, suffice to establish irreparable harm warranting a stay

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues applicant can rely on extended family and technology; mootness alone does not prove irreparable harm.

propositions.text: J. Norris noted jurisprudence on removal during pending H&C does not address removal after refusal when judicial review is pending.
propositions.quote: At paragraph 34 of Kambasaya, Justice Norris points out that the jurisprudence ... does not address the situation where the application has been refused and what is at issue is removal while a judicial review application of that decision is under consideration

paragraphs.summary: Justice Norris noted existing jurisprudence does not address removal after H&C refusal when judicial review is pending.

propositions.text: Normal consequences of deportation like family separation and cultural readjustment do not constitute irreparable harm here.
propositions.quote: Much of what the Applicant has argued ... are among the normal consequences of deportation ... I would not find that such consequences constitute irreparable harm

propositions.text: Outstanding H&C application alone is insufficient to establish irreparable harm.
propositions.quote: nor would the fact of an outstanding H&C application be sufficient

paragraphs.summary: The court finds normal deportation consequences and an outstanding H&C application do not constitute irreparable harm.

propositions.text: Removal before leave decision and judicial review would cause irreparable harm in these particular circumstances.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that ... removal before a decision on leave is made and, if granted, before the judicial review of the H&C decision is determined would constitute irreparable harm to the Applicant

paragraphs.summary: The court finds removal before leave and judicial review decisions would cause irreparable harm here.

propositions.text: Public interest favors prompt execution of removal orders, especially for serious criminality cases.
propositions.quote: the public interest generally calls for the execution of removal orders as soon as possible particularly where they concern persons who have been found to be inadmissible for serious criminality

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues public interest favors prompt removal, especially for serious criminality.

propositions.text: Public interest includes ensuring remedies are meaningful; applicant raised non-frivolous issues and faces irreparable harm if removed before consideration.
propositions.quote: there is also a public interest in ensuring that available remedies are meaningful and effective ... Applicant has raised issues ... not frivolous or vexatious and has presented a compelling case that she would suffer irreparable harm if she were to be removed before they are considered

propositions.text: The perfected application awaiting leave decision is a factor in favor of granting stay.
propositions.quote: The fact that the application has been perfected and a decision on leave will shortly be made is also a factor to be considered

paragraphs.summary: The court finds public interest includes meaningful remedies; applicant’s non-frivolous issues and perfected application favor stay.

propositions.text: Applicant has no prior criminal history, is not a reoffending risk, and remains under strict supervision pending judicial review.
propositions.quote: This is not a case where the Applicant has a long history of criminality ... she had no prior criminal history and is not considered now to be a risk to reoffend ... She will remain on parole and under strict supervision

propositions.text: Balance of convenience favors applicant; stay of removal should be granted.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the balance of convenience lies in her favour and the stay should be granted

paragraphs.summary: The court finds balance of convenience favors applicant and grants stay of removal.
